Description: The Leaflet Storymaps code template is designed to guide readers along a point-by-point tour, with a scrolling narrative to display text, images, audio, video, and scanned map backgrounds. Readers can follow the scrolling narrative or click on any marker to go directly to a specific chapter. You can create your own version by entering your map data into a linked Google Sheet (or CSV file) and uploading it into a free GitHub repository to host online. Learn more in our book, Hands-On Data Visualization.

The IBX is an abbreviation of the Interborough Express, a proposed railway line that would connect Brooklyn and Queens. It would revitalize the abandoned railway lines to allow easy transportation through the boroughs.

McDonald's Avenue's abandoned railway rests between the cross streets Elmwood Ave and Foster Ave. The McDonald's Ave street is located under the F train line and is zoned for industrial work, mostly consisting of businesses. Those businesses are centered around cars (ie car washes and rentals) along with construction materials. The residential community around McDonald's are Hasidic Jewish and were not open to talking to outsiders. However, the business owners are very different and have diverse demographic with many types of ethnic backgrounds and were open to interviews.

Media Credit: Source: US National Park Service, public domain
Description: The Ave I train stop on the F train line is the closest stop to the IBX railway. The B11 runs down this street as well as the best access Brooklyn residents have to get to this area without a car. Other bus lines run to this area but are generally far away from the Ave I station, but is decent access to the F line. However, these modes of public transportation are very hard to access due to the massive traffic problems caused by exremely outdated intersections, so busses tend to get delayed and it is faster to drive to the F train. The F train also is generally inaccessible to the communities who would use it. The main demographic of shoppers are homeowners who live on the outskirts of Brooklyn and Queens, yet the F runs to downtown Brooklyn, Manhattan, then finally Queens, but generally staying from the homeowner parts. All these combine to having inefficient public transportation despite having a lot of it.

Media Credit: Source: Anthony Citrano/Flickr, Creative Commons BY-NC-ND
Description: The intersections in McDonald's Ave are extremely problematic because of the fact it is where 3 different grids are intersecting, along with the road under the F line being extremely narrow. The Ave I intersection connects 5 different roads with odd wedges and terrible traffic lights. Along with this, the beams from the trainline along with constant construction also causes the road to be even narrower, which is a problem when large industrial cars and especially giant trucks pass through. Because traffic is so bad, along with the lack of public transportation that most people who would shop there would use, it makes the area generally inaccessible.

Media Credit: Screenshot of Zoom and Marker columns in linked Google Sheet
Description: The demographic of shoppers are mostly homeowners and contractors, with only some shops specifically for the residents (grocery stores, jewish schools, and a small mall consisting of a pharmacy, shoprite, amazing savings, etc.) However, most stores are almost exclusively catering to construction work. Right next to the tracks were many car rental, car repair, and car washes, along with construction material stores. A few blocks down is a store that has all sorts of tiles, wood, cabinets, etc for  renovations, a storage facility, and furniture stores littered everywhere. Overall, the demographic of people going to McDonald's avenue is primarily either people who already live there or those who are looking for construction materials.

Media Credit: Source: Agence France Presse/Getty Images, published by National Public Radio (2010)
Description: Of our interviews, we found the biggest concern of business owners are traffic. They all generally had similar answers to our questions about business, with the main grievances being that McDonald Ave is so inaccessible it drives away customers who would typically shop there. Because of the fact that the traffic slows everything down, one interviewee said "And then if you have to take a train, it's gonna take a long time? and then people just gonna say, 'oh, I don't want to go so far, I'm in Queens.'" He also mentioned that he lives in Queens and works in McDonald Ave, meaning that his commute is extremely long and inconvenient, and so the prospect of having an easy and convenient way to get to work excited him. This is true with other interviewees, with one who got extremely happy and mentioned that he was an uber driver before he worked at the restaurant we interviewed him at, saying that he would purposefully avoid this area because of how atrocious the traffic is.

Description:
In addition to images, you can also upload or link to audio files, which must be in one of these formats: mp3 (recommended), ogg, or wav. The template will automatically recognize audio files and allow readers to play them.

Listen to this short audio excerpt from Dr. King's 1963 speech at the Lincoln Memorial.

Description:
You can also embed a link from a streaming video service such as YouTube. Click on the YouTube video Share button, select Embed, and copy and paste only the web link, which will look similar to this:
https://www.youtube.com/embed/Q-082gadmDw

Optionally, you can add user controls and a start time to the link and make it look like this:
https://www.youtube.com/embed/Q-082gadmDw?controls=0&start=17

The Vietnam Veterans Memorial, designed by architect Maya Lin, was located near the Lincoln Memorial in 1982. Watch a portion of this video to learn more.

In addition, you can display georeferenced historical maps on top of your storymap to contrast with present-day maps. See the Overlay column in the linked Google Sheet for this chapter, and learn more in Chapter 14: Transform Your Map Data of our book.

This facsimile of Pierre (Peter) Charles L'Enfant's 1791 map, downloaded from an 1887 publication at the Library of Congress, illustrates his grand design for the permanent seat of government, which he presented to President George Washington in the early days of the new republic.

Also, you can add a GeoJSON layer of a route, boundary, or choropleth map on top of the storymap. See the GeoJSON column in the linked Google Sheet.

Media Credit: Google Sheet row number - 1 = hash number displayed in web browser.
Description:
The code template assigns each chapter a unique web address that ends with a numerical hashtag (such as ...#13). This means you can send people links to specific chapters, or refer back to another chapter in this storymap, such as this internal link to chapter 2.

Now hashtag #1 now matches your 1st row of content, immediately below the column headers, in the second row of your Google Sheet. In other words, spreadsheet row number - 1 = hashtag number.
To learn more about the Leaflet Storymaps with Google Sheets template, see our book: Hands-On Data Visualization.
